# The Department of Small Returns

The first thing I learned at the Department of Small Returns was that people rarely came in asking for what they had actually lost.

They asked for umbrellas, and meant the walk they had taken with someone who no longer spoke to them. They asked for a glove, and meant the hand that had once held theirs inside it. A man spent three Thursdays describing a silver teaspoon before admitting he wanted his sister to remember a joke. We found the spoon, eventually. His sister did not remember the joke.

This was not the department’s fault. We kept records, not miracles.

Our office occupied the ground floor of a narrow brick building between a locksmith and a bakery. The bakery sold warm rolls with sesame seeds; the locksmith kept a sign in his window that said **WE CAN OPEN ANYTHING**, a claim my supervisor, Mara, considered reckless. Our own sign was smaller: **LOST SOMETHING? INQUIRE WITHIN.** Underneath, in letters so faded they were almost invisible, someone had once added: **FOUND SOMETHING? PLEASE DO THE SAME.**

That second sentence was the reason the department worked at all.

Every morning, I opened the shutters, swept the doorstep, and emptied the brass receiving box beside the door. Into it people placed bus tickets, single earrings, photographs, buttons, keys, postcards, shopping lists, and occasionally money. Money went to the municipal office unless someone could describe the envelope it came in. Everything else received a number and a line in one of our ledgers.

The ledgers were older than the department, or so Mara said. Their pages smelled of dust and rain. On most days they behaved like ordinary books, but now and then an entry appeared in the margin that neither of us had written.

**Blue scarf, wool. Left on eastbound tram. Owner thinking of the sea.**

Or:

**One apology. Spoken too quietly at 6:14 p.m. Tuesday. Not recoverable.**

Mara believed that the city itself made these notes. I believed Mara had invented that explanation because she disliked saying she did not know.

She had worked there for forty-two years. Her hair was white, her shoes were sensible, and she could locate a misplaced bicycle bell from a customer’s description of its sound. “A city is full of people setting things down,” she told me on my first day. “Some things roll under a seat. Some things roll much farther. We help where we can.”

For eleven months, we did.

Then, one wet morning in November, a woman came in carrying an empty teacup.

She was perhaps sixty, though exhaustion made her seem older. Rain darkened the shoulders of her coat. She put the cup on the counter with both hands, as if it might escape.

“I need to find a conversation,” she said.

Mara, who had been repairing the spine of a ledger, laid down her brush. “Whose conversation?”

“Mine. With my son.”

The woman’s name was Leena Vale. Her son, Niko, had died the previous spring after a short illness. On their last afternoon together, they had sat in his kitchen drinking tea. Leena remembered the light, the loose handle on one of his cupboards, a pigeon making a terrible noise on the windowsill. She remembered that Niko had laughed.

She did not remember what he had said.

“At the time, I thought I would see him again the next day,” she told us. “I didn’t know I needed to keep every word.”

Mara offered her a chair. I brought a towel for her coat and then, after an uncertain pause, another cup of tea. Leena did not touch it. She kept her eyes on the cup she had brought, a plain white one with a small chip near the rim.

“I’ve tried everything,” she said. “I sat in his kitchen. I made the same tea. I listened to the pigeons. I can remember a hundred things he said when he was twelve, but not this.”

“We can search,” Mara said.

It was not a promise. Mara never made promises across the counter.

After Leena left, we entered the particulars in Ledger Nine. Lost conversations had their own section, though most were not truly lost. People forgot words all the time, and words went on living elsewhere—in letters, in other people, in the habits they had changed. The precise sound of an exchange was harder to trace.

“What do we look for?” I asked.

“An impression,” Mara said. “Something that held the moment.”

“The cup?”

“Perhaps. But she has the cup. Start with the things she mentioned.”

I spent the afternoon searching our shelves for a loose cupboard handle and the next morning visiting the building where Niko had lived. His landlord let me into the kitchen. The handle was still loose. When I pulled it, the cupboard door opened with a soft wooden knock. I stood there a long time, hoping the sound would summon a memory that was not mine.

Outside, pigeons crowded the ledge beneath the window. Their feathers were wet and their cries were just as dreadful as Leena had described. One of them flew up when I reached toward it, leaving a gray feather caught in the frame. I took it back to the department in a paper envelope.

Mara examined the feather, held it near her ear, and shook her head.

For six days, we found nothing.

Leena returned twice. The first time she brought the tea tin. The second time she brought a photograph of the kitchen taken at Niko’s birthday dinner, years earlier. She showed it to me across the counter. Niko had a broad face, flour on his sleeve, and an expression suggesting that someone had just told an absurd story.

“Tell me if I’m wasting your time,” she said.

“You’re not,” I said.

I wanted to tell her we would find it. Instead, I wrote down the make of the tea tin and asked whether she remembered who else had visited that day.

On the seventh morning, the ledger made an entry.

**Conversation, afternoon, one mother and one son. Misplaced at the moment of telling. See: white cup, chipped rim.**

I showed it to Mara. She closed the ledger and looked at the cup, which Leena had left with us.

There are ways to listen to objects. Most are ordinary: look for wear, smell what lingers, consider how a thing was used. Mara knew one other way. She filled the cup with water, set it in the middle of the counter, and asked me to turn off the lights.

For a while, nothing happened. Then the water trembled. A voice rose from the cup, quiet and clear.

“Do you remember the green chair?”

A woman’s voice answered, “Which green chair?”

“The one you hated. You kept saying you would throw it out, but you never did.”

“I did throw it out.”

“After I moved away.”

“It was a terrible chair.”

“It was a good chair.”

“It leaned.”

“So do I.”

There was a brief sound of laughter: his and hers, overlapping. I glanced at Mara. She was staring at the floor. The voices continued, but only as a blur now, syllables submerged beneath the small clink of china and the noise of a pigeon at the window.

Then the water went still.

We tried again. The same few sentences, the same laughter, the same blur. We could not make it yield more.

I wanted Leena to hear it immediately. Mara covered the cup with a clean cloth and said we would call her in the morning.

“Why wait?”

“Because we need to think,” she said.

“What is there to think about? We found it.”

“We found some of it.”

“That’s what she asked for.”

Mara sat down heavily. For the first time since I had known her, she looked her age. “She asked for the last conversation she had with her son. We have a piece of it. She may listen once and be glad. Or she may spend the rest of her life listening again, trying to hear through what isn’t there.”

“That should be her decision.”

“Yes,” Mara said. “It should.”

But she did not lift the cloth.

I went home angry with her. The bakery was closed when I left, and rain ran along the gutter in a silver line. I thought about all the things I could not remember: the name of the woman who taught me to swim, what my grandfather called me when I was little, the exact words my closest friend had used when she told me she was moving away. I had lived through those moments without making a record. I had no choice but to carry what remained.

Leena, though, had a choice, if we would give it to her.

The next morning I arrived early. Mara was already at the counter, writing on a slip of paper. She pushed it toward me. On it she had copied the ledger entry exactly. Beneath that she had written: **We have recovered part of the conversation. Other sounds may remain indistinct. Leena Vale may hear it if she wishes.**

“I was going to tell her,” Mara said.

“I know.”

“I just wanted one night to be certain how.”

We called Leena. She arrived before noon.

Mara explained what we had found, including the blur. Leena listened without interrupting. When Mara finished, she looked from the covered cup to me.

“Will it sound like him?”

“Yes,” I said.

She put her hands flat on the counter. “All right.”

We filled the cup. I turned off the lights.

“Do you remember the green chair?”

Leena made a sound so small I might have imagined it. She stayed motionless through the exchange, through the laughter, through the blur. When the water settled, she asked to hear it again.

We played it three times.

On the third, Leena laughed at Niko’s joke about the leaning chair. It surprised her; I could see that. She pressed a hand to her mouth and asked if she could sit for a while.

So we sat. Someone came in to ask about a set of keys, and Mara helped him quietly at the far end of the counter. Outside, people walked past our window carrying parcels and damp newspapers. Across the street, a delivery cyclist argued with a driver. The city had not paused for Leena, but she had found a little room inside its noise.

At last she said, “There was more after that.”

“Yes,” I said.

“I think he was telling me about a trip he wanted to take.” She looked at the cup. “Or maybe I was telling him about mine.”

“It might come back,” Mara said.

“It might not.”

“No.”

Leena traced the chip on the rim with her thumb. “I was so afraid I’d forgotten him. But I knew exactly when he would laugh. I remembered it before the cup got there.”

She took the cup home that afternoon. We gave her a box padded with tissue so it would be safe on the tram.

For several weeks, I expected the story to end there. I imagined her playing the conversation every evening, or putting the cup away because the voices were too painful. I learned nothing more until she returned in January with a green chair.

It was a dreadful chair. Its upholstery had faded unevenly, one leg was shorter than the others, and a tuft of stuffing escaped from a seam. Leena dragged it through the door while Mara and I watched in astonishment.

“Not the same one,” she said, catching her breath. “I found it at a secondhand shop. But it reminded me.”

She wanted to leave it in our waiting area. We had two hard wooden seats and room for one more. Mara tested the chair, felt it lean, and fetched a folded piece of cardboard to put under its short leg.

Leena sat in it first. “That’s better,” she said, though it still leaned slightly.

After she left, our visitors began choosing the green chair. Children curled up in it while their parents filled out forms. A man looking for a wedding ring fell asleep there and woke embarrassed but rested. Someone spilled coffee on one arm, and another person stitched the torn seam while waiting for news of a missing parcel.

In the spring, Leena came back to collect a striped scarf she had left on a bus. She sat in the chair while I searched the shelf of winter clothing.

“Have you listened to the cup?” I asked when I returned.

“A few times.” She wrapped the scarf around her neck. “Not lately.”

I must have looked puzzled, because she smiled.

“I know what he said about the chair.”

There were years of jokes and arguments she remembered, she told me, and recipes she still made the way Niko liked them. There were other people who had known him, too. His friends came by sometimes; together they remembered different things. One knew how he danced when he was trying to make someone laugh. Another had a recording of him singing badly at a party.

“I’m glad you found the conversation,” Leena said. “I’m also glad I don’t have to fit all of him into it.”

She went out into a mild spring rain. I watched her cross the street and disappear around the corner by the bakery.

Later that day, a boy arrived with a single red mitten. He had found it caught in the fence outside the school and wanted to make sure its owner got it back. I wrote his name in the ledger and gave the mitten a number. Before leaving, he sat in the green chair and rocked it gently from side to side.

Mara looked up from her desk. “Careful. It leans.”

“I know,” he said. “I like it.”

That evening, after we had closed, a new line appeared in the margin of Ledger Nine.

**Green chair, upholstered. Found where needed.**

Mara read it over my shoulder. “That’s a generous entry,” she said.

I thought of Leena in Niko’s kitchen, unable to know which words would be lost to her. I thought of the boy who had found a mitten and brought it somewhere a stranger might come looking. Then I opened the ledger to a clean page, ready for whatever arrived in the morning.
